title: Leros falls
pull: Five days, then the white flag

facts.text: After Italy's armistice in September 1943, British troops moved into the Italian held Dodecanese islands in the Aegean. Churchill backed the gamble: "This is a time to play high. Improvise and dare."
The Germans retook Kos in early October, leaving Leros as the main British stronghold, with about 3,000 British troops and about 5,500 Italians.
The British garrison included the 2nd Royal Irish Fusiliers, the 4th Buffs, the 1st King's Own and a company of the Royal West Kents. Brigadier Robert Tilney took command on 5 November 1943.

On 12 November German troops under Generalleutnant Friedrich Wilhelm Muller landed from the sea, and about 470 paratroopers dropped into the narrow middle of the island, cutting it in two. The German plan was called Operation Leopard.
The Luftwaffe ruled the sky. The British destroyer HMS Dulverton was sunk by German aircraft on 14 November with the loss of 78 men.
On 16 November German troops closed on Tilney's headquarters on Mount Meraviglia. Judging further resistance futile, he surrendered; Wikipedia puts it at 5:30 p.m.
About 3,200 British and 5,350 Italian soldiers were taken prisoner, more than 8,500 men in all.
About 600 British soldiers and sailors were killed or missing in the battle, many of them at sea. The Germans lost 512 killed or missing and about 900 wounded.
The Italian commander, Rear Admiral Luigi Mascherpa, surrendered at 10 p.m. that night.
Samos, the last British held island, was abandoned without a fight on 22 November. Britain's Dodecanese campaign was over.

sources.title: British POWs talk to new prisoners captured on Leros, Stalag VII A, Moosburg, IWM BU 5907 (via Wikimedia Commons)

photoNote: Covert photo taken at Stalag VII A, Moosburg, Germany: British prisoners at the barbed wire talking to newly arrived men captured on Leros. IWM BU 5907, credited to Lt W. G. Anderson, No 5 Army Film and Photographic Unit; Commons tags it PD UKGov (Crown copyright expired). Date unknown (Commons says 1944; IWM says date unknown), so it shows the aftermath, not the battle. PROBLEM: only 800 x 612 on Commons; too small for a 1600 px card. The IWM page (iwm.org.uk, object for BU 5907) returned 403 from here; Brian should download the larger IWM copy if available. Also note the photo was likely made by a prisoner and copied by the AFPU after liberation, so the Crown copyright basis is IWM's attribution; flag if in doubt. No PD photo of the battle itself was found: NARA's only Leros air photos (342-FH-3A26672 to 3A26674) show a B-17 raid of 27 November 1942, a year earlier; the Polish NAC German press photos of Leros prisoners (Commons, 2-621 to 2-626, photographer Schilling, December 1943) are tagged PD Old with no death date, which is not a clear PD basis. Faces fill the frame center; crop to the men at the wire.
photoCredit: British prisoners at Stalag VII A, Moosburg, talk to newly arrived men captured on Leros. Imperial War Museum BU 5907, public domain.

declassified.fact: For the Italians captured in the Dodecanese the worst was still to come. In February 1944 the Norwegian steamer Oria, carrying more than 4,000 Italian prisoners toward the Greek mainland, was wrecked in a storm off Cape Sounion near Athens. About 4,100 people died, one of the worst disasters at sea in the Mediterranean.

body:
Churchill's order for the Aegean was "Improvise and dare." On Leros, the dare ran out after five days.

16 November 1943. German troops closed on the headquarters of Brigadier Robert Tilney on Mount Meraviglia. Judging further resistance futile, he surrendered. The Germans had landed from the sea on 12 November and dropped about 470 paratroopers into the island's narrow waist, cutting it in two. With the Luftwaffe ruling the sky, the garrison never got its feet back under it.

About 3,200 British and 5,350 Italian soldiers were taken prisoner. Six days later Britain abandoned Samos, and its Dodecanese campaign was over. The photo shows British prisoners at a German camp talking with men newly captured on Leros.
threads:
Churchill's order for the Aegean was "Improvise and dare." On Leros, the dare ran out after five days.

16 November 1943. Cut in two by German paratroopers and pounded from the air, the British garrison surrendered. More than 8,500 British and Italian soldiers were taken prisoner, and Britain's Dodecanese campaign soon ended.
